title: Hypospadias
subject: Pathology
summary: Hypospadias is a congenital ventral displacement of the urethral meatus. Severity varies by location and chordee. Management focuses on surgical correction and monitoring for complications.

sections.p: A male newborn with the urethral opening on the ventral shaft, scrotum or perineum. Diagnosis is clinical; confirm with genital examination and assess for chordee.
b: Urethral meatus not at tip of glans
Ventral curvature (chordee) may be present

sections.p: Classify by meatal location: distal (glanular or coronal), midshaft, proximal (penoscrotal, scrotal, perineal). Proximal lesions often have severe chordee.
b: Distal – best prognosis, often single-stage repair
Proximal – may need staged repair and androgen therapy

sections.p: Mostly sporadic; multifactorial genetics and endocrine disruption. In low‑resource settings, maternal exposure to endocrine‑disrupting agents (e.g., certain herbal medicines) and infections (e.g., malaria, HIV) are reported.
b: Familial tendency (father, brother)
Maternal exposure to DES or endocrine disruptors
Associated with cryptorchidism and other GU anomalies

sections.p: Newborn or infant with abnormal urinary stream (spraying, dribbling) and visible ventral meatus. May have dorsal penile curvature and associated anomalies like undescended testes.
b: Urine stream deviates downward
Penile shaft may be tethered upward (chordee)

t.b: Confirms meatal location and chordee; guides surgical planning
Detects associated renal anomalies; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam
Rules out intersex conditions; not needed for isolated hypospadias

sections.p: Uncorrected severe chordee can impair voiding and sexual function. Urethral fistula, stricture, or infection after repair are common postoperative problems.
b: Persistent urinary obstruction
Repeated urinary tract infections
Severe curvature after puberty

sections.p: Surgical correction is definitive. Timing: 6–12 months for distal lesions, 12–18 months for proximal. Pre‑operative androgen (testosterone) may improve tissue quality in severe cases.
b: Tubularized incised plate (TIP) urethroplasty for distal disease
Two‑stage Bracka repair for proximal disease
Avoid prolonged catheterisation to reduce infection risk

sections.p: Regular post‑operative visits to assess healing, urinary stream, and penile growth. Counsel families on avoiding unnecessary catheter use and early treatment of UTIs.
b: First review at 2 weeks post‑op
Long‑term follow‑up through puberty for curvature

sections.p: Epispadias (urethral opening on dorsal penis) and posterior urethral valves (obstructive intraluminal lesion).
b: Epispadias – dorsal meatus, often with bladder exstrophy
Posterior urethral valves – obstructive leaflets, cause urinary retention

sections.p: Normal renal ultrasound does not exclude subtle collecting‑system anomalies; clinical exam remains paramount.
b: A normal scan may miss duplicated ureters that affect surgical planning

whenToSeekHelp: Severe penile pain or swelling after injury

faq.q: Why is distal hypospadias easier to repair?
faq.a: The tissue is more abundant and chordee is usually mild, allowing a single‑stage repair.

faq.q: Can hypospadias be corrected without surgery?
faq.a: No; surgery is required to create a functional urethra and correct curvature.

faq.q: Is there a genetic test for hypospadias?
faq.a: Specific genetic testing is not routine; it is used only when other intersex disorders are suspected.

exam: What are the key steps in the bedside assessment of a newborn with suspected hypospadias? — Identify meatal location, assess chordee, examine testes, look for other GU anomalies.
How does the location of the meatus influence surgical planning? — Distal lesions often need TIP repair; proximal lesions may require staged repair and pre‑operative androgen.
A child presents with a ventral meatus and severe curvature. What is the next best management? — Plan for staged repair, consider pre‑operative testosterone to improve tissue quality.
Why must you rule out posterior urethral valves before hypospadias surgery? — Valves cause obstruction; repairing hypospadias without addressing valves can lead to persistent urinary problems.
What postoperative complication should you monitor for in the first two weeks? — Urethral fistula or infection; inspect for urine leakage and signs of inflammation.
Explain why prolonged catheterisation after hypospadias repair is avoided in low‑resource settings. — Increases risk of infection and urethral trauma where sterility may be limited.
How does associated cryptorchidism affect long‑term follow‑up? — Increases risk of infertility and testicular cancer; requires orchidopexy and surveillance.
A teenager with repaired hypospadias reports a curved erection. What is the likely cause and management? — Residual chordee; consider surgical revision after puberty.
